learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels
learn.intro: Bifacial solar panels capture sunlight on both sides, boosting efficiency by up to 30%. This innovation maximizes energy output per square meter, critical for India’s land-constrained solar goals. By utilizing reflected light from surfaces like deserts or white roofs, they offer a scalable solution for urban and rural areas, accelerating the renewable transition.
learn.c1_text: These panels generate power from both front and back sides. Imagine a solar panel on a white roof reflecting sunlight underneath—it’s like having two panels in one. IRENA reports bifacial tech can increase output by 15-30%, making it ideal for arid regions like Rajasthan.
learn.c2_text: The back side relies on albedo—the reflection of light from surfaces. In deserts, sand reflects 30-40% of light, enhancing energy gain. For non-experts: think of it as a mirror boosting a flashlight’s glow. This works best with elevated installations to avoid shading.
learn.c3_text: India’s bifacial adoption is rising, especially in Gujarat and Haryana. MNRE data shows 10% of solar projects now use bifacial panels, saving 20% land compared to traditional setups. This aligns with India’s 500 GW renewable target by 2030.
learn.stat2: Bifacial panels can boost output by 30% vs. monofacial
learn.stat3: Gujarat leads bifacial adoption with 15% of projects
learn.stat4: Bifacial tech reduces land use by 20% per kW

learn.title: Electric Buses & Trucks
learn.intro: Electrifying commercial vehicles cuts emissions and fuel costs. Electric buses and trucks are key to India’s urban mobility and logistics decarbonization. With advancements in battery tech, they offer reliable, zero-emission transport for cities and freight networks, supporting national climate goals.
learn.c1_text: Electric buses produce no tailpipe pollution. A single bus can replace 30-40 diesel vehicles. For context: India’s Delhi has 4,000 electric buses, cutting 1.2 million tons of CO2 annually. It’s like swapping a gas-guzzler for a silent, clean electric car.
learn.c2_text: Modern electric trucks have ranges of 300-500 km per charge. Fast chargers can top up in 30 minutes. Think of it as a long-haul truck with a pit stop for a quick battery boost. IRENA highlights that this matches typical delivery routes, making it practical for logistics.
learn.c3_text: India’s FAME II scheme targets 70,000 electric buses by 2024. Startups like Ola Electric are deploying 15,000+ e-buses in cities. This reduces oil imports and aligns with India’s goal to hit 30% EV sales by 2030.
learn.stat2: Electric trucks can cut fuel costs by 40-60%
learn.stat3: Delhi’s e-bus fleet reduces 1.2M tons CO2/year
learn.stat4: FAME II aims for 70,000 e-buses by 2024

learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO)
learn.intro: RPO mandates DISCOMs to buy a percentage of power from renewables. This policy drives investment in solar and wind, ensuring grid stability while meeting India’s renewable targets. By requiring utilities to source clean energy, RPO accelerates the shift to a low-carbon grid.
learn.c1_text: DISCOMs must buy 33% of power from renewables by 2023. It’s like a quota system—utilities must source a chunk of their electricity from solar or wind. This policy has already led to 100 GW+ renewable capacity in India.
learn.c2_text: RPO reduces reliance on fossil fuels but raises short-term costs. DISCOMs often hedge risks via power purchase agreements (PPAs). For non-experts: imagine a restaurant required to serve 50% vegetarian dishes—it changes menu planning but ensures diversity.
learn.c3_text: India’s RPO has driven 150+ GW renewable capacity. States like Tamil Nadu meet 60% of RPO via local solar. MNRE reports that RPO compliance has reduced coal demand by 20 GW annually, easing grid pressure.
learn.stat2: 150+ GW renewable capacity driven by RPO
learn.stat4: RPO cuts coal demand by 20 GW/year

learn.title: Agrivoltaics
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics combines solar panels with farming, using the same land for both. This dual-use approach boosts agricultural productivity while generating clean energy. In India, it’s a game-changer for arid regions, providing shade for crops and water conservation benefits.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels are installed above crops, allowing sunlight to reach plants. It’s like having a greenhouse on stilts. NREL studies show a 10-20% increase in crop yields due to shade and microclimate control.
learn.c2_text: The panels create a microclimate that retains soil moisture. For example, in Rajasthan, agrivoltaics reduced irrigation needs by 30%. Think of it as a solar-powered irrigation system that also generates electricity.
learn.c3_text: India’s first agrivoltaic project in Gujarat powers 1,000 homes while supporting farming. MNRE data shows 50+ pilot projects nationwide. This aligns with India’s goal to integrate renewables with agriculture for sustainable rural development.
learn.stat2: 30% reduction in irrigation needs in Rajasthan

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)
learn.intro: A PPA is a contract where a buyer purchases renewable energy from a developer. It finances RE projects by transferring financial risk to the buyer. PPAs are vital for India’s solar and wind growth, enabling projects without upfront capital investment.
learn.c1_text: The developer builds the project, and the buyer pays a fixed price per kWh. It’s like renting a car—you pay for usage, not ownership. This model attracts investors by guaranteeing revenue for developers.
learn.c2_text: PPAs lock in prices for 15-25 years, shielding buyers from market volatility. For example, a 100 MW solar farm in India might sell power at ₹4.50/kWh via PPA. Non-experts: think of a subscription service with a fixed monthly fee.
learn.c3_text: India has 50+ GW of PPAs signed. DISCOMs use PPAs to meet RPO without upfront costs. For instance, a Maharashtra DISCOM signed a PPA for 200 MW solar, reducing its coal dependency and operational costs.
learn.stat4: PPAs reduce coal dependency by 15 GW/year

learn.title: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G)
learn.intro: V2G technology allows EVs to supply power back to the grid during peak demand. This enhances grid stability and maximizes EV battery usage. In India, V2G could transform EVs from just transport to grid assets, supporting renewable integration and reducing strain on power systems.
learn.c1_text: EVs act as mobile batteries, feeding power to the grid when needed. Imagine your car battery powering your home during a blackout. IRENA notes V2G can provide 15-20% of grid flexibility in urban areas.
learn.c2_text: V2G balances supply and demand by releasing stored energy during peaks. For non-experts: think of a rechargeable battery in your phone that also powers your laptop. This reduces the need for expensive peaking plants.
learn.c3_text: India’s EV growth (2 million+ by 2024) creates V2G opportunities. A pilot in Bengaluru showed a 10 kW V2G system stabilizing local grids. MNRE is exploring policies to incentivize V2G, aligning with India’s smart grid vision.
learn.stat4: V2G reduces peaking plant costs by 30%
